summary: The 14‑day CGM data show a hypoglycaemia‑dominant pattern, with time below range of 5.1 % and severe lows reaching 41‑42 mg/dL. The root cause is a profile ISF of 56 mg/dL/U that is far too high; even small correction doses produce large glucose drops and trigger dangerous lows. Dynamic ISF (DynISF) partially compensates but cannot fully prevent hypoglycaemia. Overnight lows at 01:00 (18.5 % TBR) and evening lows at 19:00 (15.3 % TBR) are linked to excessive sensitivity. No carbohydrate entries exist, so meal‑related parameters cannot be assessed. The AAPS automation settings are appropriate and not themselves responsible for the safety risk. The priority is to reduce the ISF to a safer value (36 mg/dL/U) and verify the improvement before any other changes.

analysis_steps.findings: CGM coverage 98.7 %, 3995 valid entries, 10 gaps ≤65 min. Profile complete with all basal, ISF, CR, target, and DIA segments. No meal entries (0 g carbs logged). AAPS profile is declared authoritative and applicable for the period.

analysis_steps.findings: Time‑below‑range 5.1 %, with multiple days >6 % (highest Aug‑18 12.8 %). Severe lows 41‑42 mg/dL on Aug‑13, Aug‑14, Aug‑21. Highest TBR at local 01:00 (18.5 %) and 19:00 (15.3 %). Coefficient of variation 32.6 %, indicating elevated variability. Any insulin‑delivery increase must be preceded by a hypoglycaemia reduction.

analysis_steps.data_gaps: No activity or meal data; some lows could be post‑exercise or post‑meal, but overnight patterns still indicate basal/ISF issue.

analysis_steps.findings: Overnight (00‑08:00) basal 0.6‑0.8 U/h: TBR 18.5 % at 01:00, average 90.6 mg/dL; TBR remains >10 % until 03:00. Evening basal 0.6‑0.7 U/h: TBR 15.3 % at 19:00, 10.1 % at 23:00. The early‑night lows suggest basal 00:00‑05:00 may be too high, or IOB from evening corrections spills over. However, without meal data, daytime TAR >15 % cannot be attributed exclusively to basal deficiency; basal and ISF errors are confounded.

analysis_steps.data_gaps: Daytime basal evaluation impossible without carbohydrate entries; influence of evening corrections on overnight lows uncertain without detailed IOB tracking.

analysis_steps.findings: CR segments cannot be evaluated (no carb data). Correction‑only boluses show that actual sensitivity is far greater than ISF 56 mg/dL/U: for example, 0.15 U from 127 mg/dL dropped 53 mg/dL in 2 h (expected ~8.4 mg/dL). Many corrections end in hypoglycaemia. This indicates ISF must be lowered. DIA of 10 h is not directly confirmable but no evidence of late‑stacking from a too‑short DIA.

analysis_steps.data_gaps: No carb data means ISF corrections might be stacked with missed meal insulin; however, the severe overtreatment pattern is consistent regardless.

analysis_steps.findings: SMB/UAM enabled, always‑enabled, temp‑target SMB active. Observed IOB rarely exceeds 6 U, well under the 25 U cap. The SMB settings themselves are safe; the dangerous lows stem from the underlying ISF error, which makes even small SMB doses overshoot.
analysis_steps.evidence: representative_loop_statuses show IOB and SMB activity. No excessive stacking. SMB doses ≤0.2 U but overlarge effect.
analysis_steps.data_gaps: No carb entries prevent evaluation of COB‑related SMB or UAM behaviour, but the always‑enabled mode is being used.

analysis_steps.findings: Dynamic ISF is active and aggressively lowering the effective ISF (variable_sens down to 27.8 mg/dL/U). This is a strong compensatory signal confirming the profile ISF is too high. Autosens disabled is appropriate. No change to automation sensitivity limits is warranted before correcting profile ISF.
analysis_steps.evidence: Loop logs with variable_sens <56. dynISF adjustment factor 70 %.

analysis_steps.findings: No declared meal strategy; zero carbohydrate entries in telemetry. Cannot evaluate pre‑bolus timing, immediate bolus percentage, or CR segments.
analysis_steps.data_gaps: Carbohydrate logging absent – essential for any meal‑bolus assessment.

analysis_steps.findings: No e‑carb entries or carbohydrate records. Assessment impossible.

The data consistently point to an ISF set too high (56 mg/dL/U) as the primary cause of both severe hypoglycaemia and excessive glucose variability. The dynamic ISF algorithm partially corrects but cannot fully compensate. The safe sequence of actions is: 1) reduce ISF to 36 mg/dL/U, 2) monitor for at least 7 days for hypoglycaemia frequency and correction behaviour, 3) after stability, begin carbohydrate logging to assess basal and CR settings, 4) only then consider basal or DIA adjustments. Automation settings should remain unchanged.
analysis_steps.data_gaps: Daytime basal and CR can be assessed only after carbohydrate logging begins.

issues: Recurrent severe hypoglycaemia (as low as 41 mg/dL) and persistently elevated time‑below‑range (5.1 % overall, overnight peaks 18.5 %).
Profile ISF of 56 mg/dL/U is far too high; actual sensitivity is roughly double, causing even 0.05‑0.2 U corrections to produce dangerous drops.
No carbohydrate logging exists – this prevents evaluation of carb ratios, meal bolus timing, and e‑carbs.
Glucose variability is high (CV 32.6 %), partly driven by the over‑correction cycle.

recommendations.title: Lower ISF to reduce hypoglycaemia risk
recommendations.description: The current ISF of 56 mg/dL/U is causing severe overtreatment. Correction boluses consistently produce drops 4‑10 times larger than expected. The system is compensating with Dynamic ISF, but hypoglycaemia still occurs. Reducing ISF to 36 mg/dL/U (a conservative step that still respects observed sensitivity) will make corrections safer and reduce the burden on dynamic adjustments.

recommendations.title: Begin carbohydrate logging to enable full profile review
recommendations.description: Without any carbohydrate entries, CR, meal timing, and e‑carb suitability cannot be assessed. Logging meals (grams and time) for at least 7 days will unlock further optimisation of the profile and meal strategy.

profile_recommendation.recommendation: Reduce ISF from 56 mg/dL/U to 36 mg/dL/U and monitor hypoglycaemia frequency and correction response for at least 7 days.
profile_recommendation.rationale: Correction boluses of 0.05‑0.2 U result in glucose drops of 26‑178 mg/dL, far exceeding the 56 mg/dL/U prediction. Observed dynamic sensitivities are as low as 27.8 mg/dL/U. A step to 36 mg/dL/U is a safe midpoint that will still allow correction while dramatically lowering hypoglycaemia risk.
profile_recommendation.next_check: After 7 days with new ISF, review glucose_min values, TBR%, and any correction reactions. If hypoglycaemia persists, consider a further ISF reduction. If daytime highs increase, potential basal adjustments can be evaluated once meal logging is started.

meal_strategy_summary.suggestion: With no carbohydrate logging, the system acts as a correction‑only loop. Begin by logging all carbohydrate intake (grams and time). Start with a short pre‑bolus of 10‑15 minutes, 100 % immediate bolus, and keep SMB/UAM enabled only after the ISF has been corrected to 36 mg/dL/U. Do not use e‑carbs until the user’s typical absorption pattern is documented.
meal_strategy_summary.rationale: Current loop behaviour is driven entirely by corrections. Without carb data, no meal‑related parameters can be tuned. A minimal, safe starting strategy avoids introducing variables that could interact with the new ISF.
meal_strategy_summary.next_observation: Log carbohydrate intake for at least 7 consecutive days, recording grams and time, to enable CR and meal‑timing analysis.

implementation_steps: 1. Safety: Discuss with healthcare team and independently verify every proposed change before acting.
2. First change: Reduce ISF from 56 mg/dL/U to 36 mg/dL/U in the AAPS profile.
3. Monitor: For at least 7 days, observe hypoglycaemia frequency (especially overnight 01:00‑03:00 and evening 19:00), correction bolus response, and time‑below‑range.
4. Only after hypoglycaemia is reduced and stable, begin entering all carbohydrate intake (grams and time) into the system.
5. Assess basal rates and CR using the new ISF and carb data. Adjust only one parameter at a time, in sequence: first basal if overnight lows persist, then CR if daytime highs remain.
6. Only after basal and CR are tuned, consider DIA adjustment if IOB stacking is observed.
7. Throughout: Make one change at a time, wait at least 3‑7 days, and verify the effect before the next change.
education: Insulin Sensitivity Factor (ISF) tells the system how much 1 unit of insulin lowers glucose. Setting ISF too high (e.g. 56 mg/dL/U when actual sensitivity is 30‑40 mg/dL/U) makes the loop underestimate insulin power and deliver too much, causing hypoglycaemia.

Dynamic ISF (DynISF) automatically adjusts the effective ISF based on recent glucose behaviour. When the profile ISF is far off, DynISF works harder to compensate, but may still not prevent extreme lows.
Small correction doses (0.05‑0.2 U) can be dangerous with high sensitivity; a tiny miscalculation leads to large glucose drops. Fixing ISF makes every dose safer.
Carbohydrate logging is essential for a closed‑loop system to bolus for meals and use e‑carbs effectively. Without it, the system is blind to food and can only correct after the fact.
safety_notes: This is decision‑support content only. The user must independently verify every proposed change, make changes one at a time, and monitor glucose closely.
Severe hypoglycaemia has been recorded (41‑42 mg/dL). Do not increase any insulin‑delivery setting until hypoglycaemia frequency is reduced.
After reducing ISF, always keep fast‑acting carbohydrates available and watch for unexpected lows, especially overnight.
Consult with a healthcare professional before making profile changes, and ensure all caregivers are aware of the new settings.
